mcqs.question: What is the first step in applying OCP correctly to a growing conditional?
options: Add a generic plugin framework immediately, regardless of what varies
Rewrite the conditional as a lookup table without further analysis
Name the actual axis of variation — what specifically keeps growing new cases — and put the extension point exactly there
Split the function into smaller functions of equal size
mcqs.explanation: OCP is only useful when the extension point targets the dimension that actually varies — naming that axis first prevents building the wrong abstraction. A generic framework, a bare lookup-table conversion, or splitting by size alone don't address the real question of what needs to extend without being told to.

mcqs.question: Comparing the switch-statement version and the class-per-tier version when adding a fifth shipping tier, what's the key visual difference?
options: The switch version's change touches one shared, already-used function everywhere it's called; the class-per-tier version's change touches nothing that existed before
The class-per-tier version requires more total lines of code, which makes it strictly worse
The switch version is always faster at runtime regardless of tier count
There is no meaningful difference once the change is deployed to production
mcqs.explanation: The switch version edits a function every existing call site already depends on, risking a regression across all of them; the class-per-tier version adds a wholly new file with zero edits to existing, tested code. Line count and runtime speed aren't the point being illustrated, and the risk difference is very real, not cosmetic.

mcqs.question: How much abstraction should you build before a second shipping-tier variant actually exists?
options: None at all — even the interface should wait until a second variant exists
Only the interface itself, since defining it costs almost nothing even with one implementation; hold off on registry or dispatch machinery until a second variant justifies it
The full registry and dispatch machinery, built ahead of time to save effort later
A complete plugin framework with configuration loading and hook ordering
mcqs.explanation: A one-method interface costs nothing extra since you were writing a class either way, and it's cheap to build even before a second implementation exists — but generic dispatch or registry machinery is worth deferring until real evidence justifies its shape. Skipping the interface too is overly cautious, and building the full framework upfront repeats the YAGNI-gone-wrong mistake.

mcqs.question: Why is pre-building a generic extension point for an axis that has never actually varied considered the wrong move?
options: Because extension points are always a code smell regardless of context
Because it always makes the code run measurably slower
Because OCP forbids the use of interfaces entirely
An extension point built on a guess rather than an observed pattern of variation usually guesses the wrong shape, the same failure mode as a speculative plugin framework
mcqs.explanation: Without an observed or concretely imminent pattern of variation, the abstraction's shape is a guess, and guesses about future variation are usually wrong in the same way the YAGNI-vs-extensibility failure mode plays out. Extension points aren't inherently a smell, OCP relies on interfaces rather than forbidding them, and this isn't primarily a performance claim.
